Article Title: Ukraine strikes Russian oil refinery, passenger train in overnight drone attacks; 2 dead
Article Text:
The Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery in Russia's southern Rostov region was also damaged in the attacks.

Oil refinery forced to halt operations

Passenger train hit in Samara

Two people were killed in separate Ukrainian drone attacks across Russia overnight, Russian officials said, as the strikes damaged an oil refinery, industrial sites and a passenger train.Russia's defence ministry said its air defences destroyed 592 Ukrainian drones during the overnight barrage, reported news agency Reuters.One person was killed and another injured in Belgorod after a Ukrainian drone struck a truck, according to local officials. In Perm, Governor Dmitry Makhonin said one person was killed during what he described as a large-scale drone attack. The region is home to a major oil refinery.The Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery in Russia's southern Rostov region was also damaged in the attacks.Governor Yuri Slyusar said around 50 drones were destroyed over the region and the strike forced the refinery to temporarily suspend operations. He said there were no reports of casualties there.In Ulyanovsk, eight people were injured after another drone attack damaged industrial and civilian infrastructure, Governor Alexei Russkikh said.The region is home to a major electronics plant.A passenger train travelling from Moscow to Tolyatti was also damaged in the overnight attacks.Russia's state railway operator said an electric locomotive and the train's first carriage were damaged by what it described as external interference on a section of railway in the Samara region.The train driver was injured and rail traffic on the affected section was temporarily suspended.In the Voronezh region, Governor Alexander Gusev said air defences destroyed 88 drones over the regional capital and at least six surrounding districts.Four people were injured there, while residential buildings, vehicles and industrial facilities were damaged, Gusev said.
Article Summary: One person killed and another injured in Belgorod after a Ukrainian drone struck a truck. In Perm, one person was killed during what he described as a large- scale drone attack. The Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery in Russia's southern Rostov region was also damaged.

Article Title: Colorado researchers grew the world's most expensive spice on rooftop solar panels; harvested twice the output and generated $60,000 in return while producing electricity
Article Text:
A sunlit experiment

A $60,000 figure

There are no limits to what a well-planned project cannot achieve and researchers in Colorado have proven it right. They have managed to make a rooftop with solar panels produce electricity while also growing the world's most expensive spice and generating extra income.Colorado State University researchers report that saffron, grown beneath solar panels rated at 40% transparency, produced twice as many flowers and twice the dried spice yield as compared to unshaded rooftop plots. The conditions on a green roof – well-drained, nutrient-poor substrates and extreme microclimates – are surprisingly ideal for saffron production. The finding points to a promising use of agrovoltaics, which pairs agriculture with solar electricity generation.The research was conducted at the CSU Spur campus in Denver, where Jennifer Bousselot's team studies planted roofs with and without solar installations. These spaces let researchers investigate how urban rooftops could produce food where farmland remains scarce. It was in 2007 that Bousselot began studying the relationship between green roofs and solar panels.In their March 2026 research summary, Reece Bailey and Bousselot warn that “too much shade can be detrimental to saffron yield.”They propose panels that transmit 30% to 40% of the light, mounted 6 to 8 feet above the growing surface.A separate 2022 experiment in eastern Morocco compared full sun with three shade levels over 24 months and found the highest saffron yield with 30% shade. That is roughly 70% of sunlight remaining, not 30% transmission. The percentages describe different things, so the studies do not establish one universal lighting recipe for every climate and panel layout.The Colorado team modelled five years on an existing 46-kilowatt rooftop array with 4,356 square feet of growing space. Its budget projects about $61,000 in net revenue, including electricity, dried saffron, and sales of corms (the underground structures used to grow new plants).The assumptions include $35 per gram of saffron and corms at 25 cents each. Electricity can contribute $13,470 over the five years. However, first-year costs exceed revenue and the budget does not cover building a new rooftop installation.Saffron consists of the dried red stigmas of Crocus sativus, a fall-blooming crocus harvested and processed by hand. That careful work helps explain why a tiny jar in the kitchen can carry such a large price tag.University of Vermont researchers measured just how much work sits behind the harvest. In their solar-field experiment, producing a single gram of dried saffron required 159 to 179 flowers. A larger flower count is encouraging, but it also means more flowers to pick and process before that spice reaches a customer. The timing can be useful for small farms, too. Vermont’s saffron researchers describe an October or November harvest, after much of the main growing-season rush has passed. The crop could provide additional seasonal income, although someone still has to pick the flowers and separate the delicate threads.For cities, the appeal of the project is exciting. Rooftop farming and solar generation can share the space and panel shade can reduce crop heat stress and irrigation needs under suitable conditions. CSU Extension notes that rooftop systems present installation and maintenance challenges, with planting and harvesting done by hand. In practical terms, a productive roof needs more than plants and panels. It needs a workable plan for growing, harvesting, and maintaining both systems.
Article Summary: Colorado State University researchers report that saffron, grown beneath solar panels rated at 40% transparency, produced twice as many flowers and twice the dried spice yield as compared to unshaded rooftop plots. The finding points to a promising use of agrovoltaics, which pairs agriculture with solar electricity generation.

Article Title: Oregon feared a famous 92-foot waterfall on private land could be sold to a new owner; the state has now approved a $2 million purchase that will permanently protect Abiqua Falls and open public acces
Article Text:
The waterfall drops 92 feet into a pool surrounded by ferns, moss-covered rocks and a basalt cliff

The sale of Abiqua Falls

Lawmakers backed public ownership

State has to prepare the site

Oregon has approved a $2 million purchase of Abiqua Falls, ending concerns that the famous 92-foot waterfall could remain in private hands after its owner put the property up for sale earlier this year. The deal includes the waterfall and 160 acres of land in Marion County, with the state planning to protect the site and provide public access.The Oregon State Parks and Recreation Commission approved the sale from the Abbey Foundation of Oregon on Wednesday, KGW8 reported. The foundation had owned the property for more than 100 years and put it up for sale in February, raising concerns among members of the public and lawmakers about what could happen to the popular natural landmark if it went to another private owner.Abiqua Falls is located near Scotts Mills, east of Salem. The waterfall drops 92 feet into a pool surrounded by ferns, moss-covered rocks and a basalt cliff. People have visited the site for decades even though the land itself was privately owned.The agreement now moves the property towards public ownership. The purchase is expected to close around the end of 2026, according to Oregon State Parks and Recreation Department (OPRD).The agency is also working on options for how the property will be managed and developed.The Abbey Foundation of Oregon, the fundraising organisation connected to Mount Angel Abbey and Seminary, had owned Abiqua Falls for more than a century. When the property was listed for sale in February, Oregon lawmakers moved to find a way to keep the waterfall in public hands.An earlier proposal reported by Oregon Public Broadcasting included $2.1 million for the acquisition. That proposal covered $600,000 for the Abiqua Falls property and $1.4 million for another 160 acres of nearby rapids and forestland owned by timber company Weyerhaeuser.The latest agreement approved by the Oregon State Parks and Recreation Commission is for $2 million and includes the 92-foot waterfall and 160 acres of unmaintained trails.The Abbey Foundation said it was handing over responsibility for the site with the hope that it would remain accessible for future generations."It is with deep gratitude and hope for the future that the Abbey Foundation of Oregon entrusts the stewardship and legacy of Abiqua Falls to the state of Oregon,” said Dr Amanda Staggenborg, director of communications for Mount Angel Abbey. "The beauty of Abiqua Falls will be enjoyed by generations of Oregonians and all those who love Oregon’s natural wonders," she added.The effort to acquire the waterfall received support from lawmakers from both political parties. They pursued the purchase through a general obligation bond to bring the property into public ownership.House Majority Leader Ben Bowman said the purchase would allow future generations to visit the waterfall themselves. "Today, we are making sure that our children and grandchildren inherit not just stories about Abiqua Falls, but the ability to stand there themselves," Bowman said. "This place should belong to all of us. Oregon owes a debt of gratitude to the Abbey Foundation for their century of stewardship, and their partnership in ensuring public access forever," he added.The move followed months of discussion about the future of the waterfall after its sale was proposed. Earlier in March, lawmakers had said several details still needed to be settled, including which state agency would manage the property and how public access would work.Buying the waterfall is only the beginning of bringing the property under state management. The land currently includes unmaintained trails, meaning the state will have to determine how the site can be managed and brought up to the standards expected of a public park.OPRD director Lisa Sumption said owning a natural site also means taking on the work needed to maintain it. "Abiqua Falls is a great example that parks are not just nature. It takes continuous staff, time and money for us to bring a property like this up to state park standards and keep it there," Sumption said.The agency has not yet announced a final management plan for the property. The state is expected to continue assessing how the land should be developed and maintained while working towards the completion of the purchase.Once the sale is completed, Oregon will take responsibility for the property and work towards ensuring that Abiqua Falls remains accessible to the public.
Article Summary: The sale includes the 92-foot waterfall and 160 acres of land in Marion County. The Abbey Foundation of Oregon had owned the property for more than 100 years and put it up for sale in February. The sale ends concerns about what could happen to the popular natural landmark if it went to another private owner.

Article Title: About 51,000 battery packs used inside reclining chairs are being recalled after reports of overheating, smoking and igniting; the packs were sold on Amazon for about $105 for more than three years
Article Text:
How to identify the recalled battery

What should you do?

The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) has recalled approximately 51,000 lithium-ion battery packs used in reclining chairs after reports of the batteries overheating and catching fire. The recalled product is Blue Cactus Company's 2,500 mAh battery pack (model RWX-RBP02), which was sold on Amazon from May 2023 through July 2026.The agency said it received four reports of the batteries overheating, smoking or igniting. Though there are only a small number of reported cases, lithium-ion batteries still carry dangers when they fail. They can ignite suddenly and are difficult to extinguish once they start burning. The recall announcement was made on Thursday (September 24).The recalled products are black battery packs with ‘The Blue Cactus Company’ branding and logo printed on the front. The recalled product bears the model number RWX-RBP02 on the rear. These batteries were designed to power various reclining chair brands, meaning they may have been sold alongside different manufacturers' furniture or as replacement parts.If you purchased a reclining chair battery pack from Amazon between May 2023 and July 2026 for around $105, it is important that you check the battery against the model number. The product is fairly distinctive: it comes with a black casing, and the branding is unmistakable. Look for the model number to know whether your battery falls under this recall.If your recliner has the recalled battery, it is important that you stop using it right away and contact The Blue Cactus Company for a replacement. The company said it is offering free replacements for the recalled product. You may need to reference your purchase receipt or product information when reaching out.In the meantime, remove the battery pack from your reclining chair and store it away from living areas, ideally in a cool, dry place away from other flammable materials.“Do not throw this recalled lithium-ion battery or device in the trash, the general recycling stream (e.g., street-level or kerbside recycling bins), or in used battery recycling boxes found at various retail and home improvement stores,” the CPSC said.The agency urged that the recalled lithium-ion batteries must be disposed of differently from other batteries, as they present a greater risk of fire. “Your municipal household hazardous waste (HHW) collection centre may accept this recalled lithium-ion battery or device for disposal. Before taking your battery or device to a HHW collection centre, contact it ahead of time and ask whether it accepts recalled lithium-ion batteries. If it does not, contact your municipality for further guidance,” the agency added.The recalled battery packs were imported by Go North Rocket 28 AB, a company based in Sweden. They were sold exclusively through Amazon during the three-year window. You can contact the manufacturer directly or work through Amazon customer service if you still have your order history.If you have the recalled batteries, the safest approach is to treat them as a potential hazard until you have obtained a replacement. Check your Amazon order history if you cannot recall whether you own one of these packs. The model number RWX-RBP02 is the specific identifier to verify. If you find one in your home, do not use it, and begin the process of getting it replaced and properly disposed of.
Article Summary: The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission has recalled approximately 51,000 lithium-ion battery packs used in reclining chairs. The recalled product is Blue Cactus Company's 2,500 mAh battery pack (model RWX-RBP02), which was sold on Amazon from May 2023 through July 2026. The agency said it received four reports of the batteries overheating, smoking or igniting.

Article Title: The US has returned 36 ancient Syrian artifacts worth more than $5 million; 13 were seized from the Metropolitan Museum of Art, a Palmyra stone relief, 14 Roman mosaics were among the objects sent hom
Article Text:
The collection also includes 14 mosaics taken from a Roman villa in Syria. Among the other notable pieces is a third-century BCE mosaic section portraying the mythological wedding of Telete and Eros, created from hundreds of tiny pieces of colored stone known as tesserae.

A collection spanning centuries

13 pieces came from the Met

Tracing a global antiquities trade

Ancient pieces of Syrian history that had traveled far from their original landscapes are now making the journey back home. US authorities have returned 36 antiquities to Syria, a collection worth more than $5 million that includes a monumental relief from Palmyra, Roman-era mosaics and objects recovered from major private and institutional collections, states a report by Arab News. The repatriation, announced September 23, marks another major effort to trace and recover cultural objects that entered the international art market through illicit trafficking.According to Arab News, among the returned objects is a massive limestone relief from ancient Palmyra. The funerary sculpture dates to the late second century CE and depicts a reclining man surrounded by a woman and three children. Weighing more than 1,000 pounds, the relief originally formed part of a Palmyrene tomb. Investigators determined that it had been carefully removed from a burial chamber before being smuggled through Dubai.Its history is particularly significant because the relief left Palmyra before the ancient city suffered extensive destruction at the hands of ISIS between 2015 and 2017. The archaeological site, a UNESCO World Heritage site, was heavily damaged during the conflict, making the recovery of objects removed from the city especially important.The collection also includes 14 mosaics taken from a Roman villa in Syria. Among the other notable pieces is a third-century BCE mosaic section portraying the mythological wedding of Telete and Eros, created from hundreds of tiny pieces of colored stone known as tesserae.The report adds that thirteen of the 36 antiquities were seized from the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York as part of investigations into the provenance of ancient objects held by the institution.The Manhattan District Attorney's Office said its Antiquities Trafficking Unit has seized 402 antiquities from the Met since 2017, with a combined value of $98.7 million. The Syrian return therefore forms part of a much broader examination of objects that passed through museums, galleries and private collections.Four other objects in the latest repatriation came from the collection of American collector Michael Steinhardt. Those pieces were among approximately 180 antiquities valued at $70 million that authorities recovered from his collection in a 2021 agreement. That agreement also resulted in a lifetime prohibition on his acquiring additional antiquities.Investigators linked 31 of the returned Middle Eastern and North African antiquities to objects allegedly trafficked into New York by Georges Lotfi, a Lebanese antiquities dealer who is the subject of an arrest warrant issued in 2022 and an Interpol Red Notice from 2023. The allegations against him remain subject to the legal process.The latest return adds Syria to a growing list of countries receiving cultural artifacts recovered through investigations in New York. The Manhattan District Attorney's Antiquities Trafficking Unit says it has recovered more than 6,400 cultural treasures valued at about $495 million and returned more than 6,200 of them to 40 countries.For Syria, the return represents the recovery of objects connected to civilizations that flourished thousands of years ago, and, in the case of the Palmyra relief, a tangible piece of a site whose surviving heritage has faced extraordinary losses in recent history, concludes the report.
Article Summary: US authorities have returned 36 antiquities to Syria, a collection worth more than $5 million that includes a monumental relief from Palmyra. The repatriation, announced September 23, marks another major effort to trace and recover cultural objects that entered the international art market through illicit trafficking.

Article Title: A silver US Army ring missing since 2006 was found in another soldier’s footlocker; after a three-year search, a Fort Worth woman finally returned it to its original owner 20 years later
Article Text:
A mystery ring

Back to the owner

Sheppard shared that he had not seen the ring since 2006. Image credit: NBC 5 Responds

A silver US army ring that had been missing for two decades is back with the soldier who once wore it, completing a promise a Fort Worth woman made about three years ago. In 2023, when Mary Thelen found the ring, she told NBC 5 Responds that she would keep looking for its owner.She had found the possession tucked inside an old footlocker belonging to her son, Douglas, who served four tours in Iraq. Douglas did not remember exactly where he found it, thinking it might have been overseas, either in a truck or somewhere in the sand near Baghdad.Finding the owner was made a tad bit easy with the clues on the ring itself. Texas, four aces, the nickname 'T-Bone' and most importantly a name engraved on it: Terry Sheppard Jr. When the outlet shared Thelen's story first in February 2023, it attracted plenty of attention. Online sleuths began contacting a man by that name.“I had a lot of people messaging me on Facebook, just randomly,” Sheppard recalled. “One of my coworkers told me about a story they’d seen, and they were like, ‘You think that’s yours?’” For a while, it seemed the mystery had been solved, but Sheppard and Thelen never connected and the ring remained in her care.But Thelen did not calm down in her efforts and kept searching for the ring's rightful owner. “I can see that this ring belongs to a person who really wants it back, and I really want to meet him,” she said.Then, during the summer of 2026, Sheppard reached out to NBC 5 seeking help recovering his ring. A few weeks later he and Thelen met each other. “See if you remember that,” Thelen said as she handed him the ring. “Oh, my goodness,” Sheppard replied. “I haven’t seen this in forever.”Sheppard shared that he had not seen the ring since 2006. He ordered it after completing basic training. The design was a personal snapshot of the young soldier he was at the time, featuring his name, his Texas roots and his nickname, 'T-Bone'. “I’m glad it’s back where it belongs,” Thelen told him.While the owner was revealed, what still remained a mystery was how the ring reached somewhere in Iraq. Sheppard never deployed to Iraq, meaning Douglas could not have found the ring there. Moreover, Sheppard added that he had only worn it once or twice. “The last place I can remember having my ring would be Fort Bragg, North Carolina, 82nd Airborne Unit,” he said.It turns out Douglas was also stationed at Fort Bragg during that period. Both men worked in the same area. Sheppard believes he may have removed the ring while working. Douglas likely found it and forgot about it, until his mother uncovered it many years later.Whether Terry and Douglas ever crossed paths remains unknown. “I just never thought I’d actually see this again,” Sheppard said.
Article Summary: A silver US army ring that had been missing for two decades is back with the soldier who once wore it, completing a promise a Fort Worth woman made about three years ago. In 2023, when Mary Thelen found the ring, she told NBC 5 Responds that she would keep looking for its owner. She had found the possession tucked inside an old footlocker belonging to her son, Douglas, who served four tours in Iraq.

Article Title: In 1995, Selena’s family made an agreement over profits from her entertainment legacy; 31 years later, brother A.B. Quintanilla is suing sister Suzette for more than $1 million he says he is owed
Article Text:
Selena’s 1995 family agreement; 31 years later, A.B. sues Suzette over $1M in profits (Image Credit: Getty and AP)

The agreement dates back to 1995

The companies managing Selena’s legacy

When A.B. says he discovered the problem

Suzette and Marcella dispute the allegations

Selena’s legacy remains a family business

What A.B. is asking the court to decide

More than three decades after Selena Quintanilla’s death, a dispute over the business built around her music and legacy has moved into court. According to court documents obtained by ABC13, Selena’s brother Abraham “A.B. ” Quintanilla III has sued his sister, Suzette Quintanilla Arriaga, along with two companies connected to the family’s entertainment business. Filed in Nueces County, Texas, the lawsuit alleges that a family agreement made after Selena’s 1995 death entitled A.B. to 25% of profits from certain entertainment properties. He is seeking more than $1 million, along with an accounting of the estate’s finances.Selena was killed in March 1995 at the age of 23. In the months following her death, members of her family entered into what the lawsuit describes as the “Estate Properties Agreement”. According to the court documents, the agreement involved A.B., Suzette, their mother Marcella Quintanilla and Selena’s husband, Christopher Pérez. A.B. says the agreement made him a party to the arrangement and an intended beneficiary.The lawsuit states that he was entitled to receive 25% of the net profits generated by certain entertainment properties connected with Selena. Those interests include aspects of her name, image, likeness, voice, commercial ventures and broader intellectual property.Her music, image and name have continued to generate commercial activity decades after her death.A key part of the dispute involves two companies named in the lawsuit: Q Production, Inc. and Q Productions, Inc. The court filing says Q Production, Inc. was established by Selena’s father, Abraham Quintanilla Jr., after her death to handle aspects of her entertainment affairs. Suzette later created Q Productions, Inc. in 2025. According to the lawsuit, the newer company became a principal entity through which Selena’s entertainment affairs, intellectual-property rights, commercial ventures and legacy were managed.A.B. alleges that Suzette eventually exercised control over the business activities covered by the family agreement. His lawsuit claims that this resulted in him not receiving the full share of profits to which he believes he was contractually entitled.The lawsuit places particular emphasis on 2025. A.B. says he discovered in spring 2025 that he had not received all of the money he believed he was owed. He then sought financial information that would allow him to determine how much had been generated and how much of that amount should have been paid to him.According to the filing, he requested access to financial records but says the information was not provided. The dispute therefore involves more than the amount A.B. is seeking. His lawsuit also asks for a detailed accounting covering Selena’s estate and related business activity. The filing seeks records dating from 2016 through the present, as well as more than $1 million in unpaid profits and proceeds. A.B. is also seeking attorney fees and court costs.The allegations have been disputed by Suzette and their mother, Marcella Quintanilla. In a joint statement posted on Selena’s official social media account before the lawsuit was formally filed, the two rejected suggestions that Suzette had stolen or improperly taken money or property belonging to A.B., other family members, Selena’s estate or jointly owned family businesses. They also questioned A.B.’s earlier public references to a lawsuit and alleged wrongdoing involving their late father. At the time of that statement, they said they had not found a publicly filed case matching the description A.B. had given.The subsequent court filing in Nueces County has now established that A.B. has filed a civil lawsuit naming Suzette and the two companies. The family’s earlier response nonetheless remains relevant to the dispute because it shows that the allegations were contested before the case became public through the court documents.The dispute comes against the backdrop of a legacy that has grown considerably since Selena’s death. During her lifetime, Selena performed with Selena y Los Dinos, the family band in which both A.B. and Suzette also played. A.B. became an important songwriter and producer for the group, while Suzette played drums before later becoming involved in the business surrounding her sister’s legacy.After Selena’s death, her music and image continued to be used across recordings, merchandise, licensing, entertainment projects and other commercial ventures. Managing her estate and intellectual property has remained central to the family’s business activities. Her father, Abraham Quintanilla Jr., who had played a central role in managing Selena’s career, died in December 2025 at age 86. The lawsuit now raises questions about the financial arrangements governing the estate after his death.The lawsuit does not simply seek a payment. A.B. is asking for financial records that would establish how much money was generated from the relevant entertainment properties and determine what portion he believes he is entitled to receive under the 1995 agreement. He is seeking more than $1 million in unpaid profits, an accounting covering the relevant period, and reimbursement for legal expenses and court costs.The case now puts a decades-old family agreement under scrutiny while the business surrounding Selena’s name and legacy continues. For A.B., the central issue is whether the terms agreed upon after Selena’s death were followed and whether he received the share of profits and financial information he says the agreement provides.
Article Summary: Abraham ‘A.B.’ Quintanilla III has sued his sister, Suzette Quintanillas Arriaga, along with two companies connected to the family’s entertainment business. The lawsuit alleges that a family agreement made after Selena's 1995 death entitled A.B to 25% of profits from certain entertainment properties. Suzette and their mother, Marcella, dispute the allegations.

Article Title: ‘Long skirts, good mothers': Italian minister sparks outrage over sexist remarks
Article Text:
Italian minister apologises after remarks linking skirt length to marriage

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is most important when discussing gender expectations in society? Personal freedom Equal opportunities Individual choices Respect for different perspectives 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Italy’s foreign minister Antonio Tajani has faced backlash after suggesting that women who wear longer skirts are more suitable for marriage and more likely to make good mothers.“My children are married,” he said. “But if I had to advise a young man which woman to marry, I would suggest a less flashy but more reliable, more serious woman, who will certainly be a good mother.“Ready to provide the necessary answers, always present. Perhaps less pretty, with a slightly longer skirt. But while with the attractive one you might get a few ‘cornettos’, with the other you are certainly sure of everlasting love. She will keep her promise to marry and ensure the stability of the home. She will be there.," he added.The 73-year-old deputy prime minister later apologised for the remarks, which he made during a political event on Friday. His comments sparked strong criticism from politicians across Italy, with former prime minister and current Florence Senator Matteo Renzi calling them “backwards”.Renzi also shared an AI-generated image of Tajani wearing a short denim mini-skirt in a satirical response to his remarks.Addressing the controversy on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly this week, Tajani said he had been “misunderstood” and apologised for any offence his remarks may have caused, according to comments reported by Italian media.“I apologise if people felt offended by what I said, but I never intended to offend women, and I never have, either in my private or my public life,” he said.The controversy comes as Italy prepares to ban the burqa and niqab in schools, with Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announcing on Sunday that her government would soon take the measure to the Cabinet.Meloni also proposed limiting the number of foreign students in each classroom and requiring parents of foreign students facing serious integration difficulties to learn Italian. The government has not yet specified the proposed limit on foreign students.
Article Summary: Antonio Tajani said women who wear longer skirts are more suitable for marriage and more likely to make good mothers. The 73-year-old deputy prime minister later apologised for the remarks, which he made during a political event on Friday. He said he had been ‘misunderstood’ and apologised for any offence his remarks may have caused.

Article Title: Iran offers US 7-day plan to end war, reopen Strait of Hormuz
Article Text:
The Strait of Hormuz has emerged as a central bargaining point in efforts to end the conflict

Tehran seeks phased route out of war

Iran has offered the United States a seven-day plan to end the nearly seven-month war in West Asia, with Tehran proposing that the Strait of Hormuz be reopened by the end of the seventh day if certain conditions are met, The New York Times reported.Under the proposal, Iran would reopen the strategic waterway and the US and Iran would restart comprehensive negotiations over Tehran’s nuclear programme. Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi said the proposal had been conveyed to Washington through intermediaries and was similar to a memorandum of understanding reached by the two sides in June.“We have introduced a plan to the United States through the intermediators that if certain conditions are met, the Strait of Hormuz would be open on the end of the seventh day and talks would restart...it would be better, if a deal was reached before the U.S. midterm elections,” Araghchi told reporters at the United Nations General Assembly, according to the report.The proposal comes as both sides remain publicly committed to diplomacy but sharply divided over the terms of any settlement. US President Donald Trump has threatened to “annihilate” Iran if no agreement is reached, while also indicating that a deal could be possible.The Strait of Hormuz has emerged as a central bargaining point in efforts to end the conflict. Reuters, citing Iranian, regional and Western diplomatic sources, reported that negotiators in New York were exploring a phased arrangement under which Iran would reopen the waterway in return for the US lifting its economic blockade.A senior Iranian official said a possible arrangement could begin with an end to the US blockade and the reopening of Hormuz, followed potentially by access to frozen Iranian assets. The sources said the main difficulty was that neither side wanted to surrender its leverage first.The negotiations also face the challenge of ensuring that any agreement is durable enough to prevent a repeat of an earlier understanding that collapsed in July. Trump has said he believes a deal could potentially be reached after the November 3 US midterm elections.A White House official, however, said Trump remained open to talks only “under the right circumstances”, while arguing that Washington was in a strong negotiating position because of the pressure on Iran's economy and the situation around Hormuz.
Article Summary: Iran has offered the United States a seven-day plan to end the nearly seven- month war in West Asia. Tehran proposes that the Strait of Hormuz be reopened by the end of the seventh day if certain conditions are met. Under the proposal, Iran would reopen the strategic waterway and the US and Iran would restart comprehensive negotiations.

Article Title: 19-year-old lost his lamp in an Australian cave in 1953, survived three days, became a NASA scientist; 68 years later, students found the lamp still hanging
Article Text:
Professor Brian O’Brien and the carbide lamp he lost inside an Australian cave in 1953. Image: ABC

A short cave trip turned into a 75-hour survival ordeal

The lost lamp remained in the cave for decades

Britanny Meers who recovered the lamp

Two students spotted the lamp 68 years after it was lost

Volunteer cavers spent two hours reaching it in 2026

The teenager became a NASA scientist and the lamp will now be displayed

Brian O’Brien was 19 when he entered the Yarrangobilly Caves in New South Wales in December 1953 with fellow caver Fred Stewart, but a short exploration turned into a three-day fight for survival. The pair became separated inside East Deep Cave, and O’Brien eventually lost the carbide lamp that was his only source of light after slipping and falling. He spent about 74 to 75 hours underground with little food and only a small amount of water before rescuers found him. O’Brien later became a NASA scientist and worked on lunar dust experiments carried aboard Apollo missions. His abandoned lamp remained inside the cave for decades. In 2021, two students discovered it about 60 metres underground, still hanging from a rocky ledge, before a volunteer caving team recovered it in 2026.O’Brien and Stewart were members of the Sydney University Speleological Society and had travelled to Yarrangobilly after finishing their university examinations. On December 15, 1953, they explored West Deep Creek Cave before deciding to have a quick look inside East Deep Creek Cave on their way back to camp.As their carbide lamps began running low, they started making their way towards the entrance, but O’Brien stayed behind to investigate another section. He became disoriented and was left alone in an unfamiliar part of the cave. His lamp eventually failed, leaving him in darkness. During his attempt to find a way out, he hooked the lamp onto a rock wall, then slipped and fell and could no longer locate it. He eventually heard rescuers after about 75 hours underground.O’Brien survived his ordeal, but the lamp stayed behind in the cave. For decades, it became a small but memorable part of his story, particularly because he continued to want it recovered. O’Brien's daughter, Ros O’Brien, told ABC that her father never stopped looking for the lamp and always wanted to bring it back. Brian O’Brien died in 2020 at the age of 86, meaning he did not live to see the object found. The NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service later said the lamp remained undiscovered for more than 70 years, while the exact location of the object was eventually identified by a new generation of cavers.The lamp was finally spotted in 2021 by Brittany Meers and her friend Lachlan Bailey, who were students and exploring the cave as cavers. They found the relic roughly 60 metres underground, where it was hanging from a high ledge. At the time, they did not immediately understand its historical significance and left it in place. The discovery later became known within the caving community, prompting discussions about how it could be safely recovered while respecting the cave environment and the O’Brien family's wishes. The finding came 68 years after O’Brien had lost the lamp during his 1953 ordeal, creating the second chapter of a story that had begun more than six decades earlier.Four volunteer cavers, including Meers, returned to the cave in 2026 to retrieve the lamp under a recovery mission coordinated with NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service. The route was difficult, with the team squeezing through narrow spaces and scrambling across challenging sections in temperatures that could fall to about 5 degrees Celsius. Although the lamp was only about 100 to 150 metres into the cave in a straight line, the obstacles made the journey considerably more difficult. After about two hours underground, the group reached the lamp and successfully removed it from the rock where it had remained since 1953. The object was reportedly in remarkably good condition, with surprisingly little corrosion after more than seven decades underground.The recovered lamp became an unexpected link between two very different parts of O’Brien's life. After surviving his cave ordeal, he went on to become a prominent space scientist specialising in lunar dust. An Australian government citation records that O’Brien served as a NASA principal investigator, invented the Apollo Dust Detector Experiment and developed experiments that were deployed on Apollo missions including Apollo 11, 12, 14 and 15. His family has entrusted the recovered lamp to NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service, which plans to preserve and display it at Yarrangobilly. Ros O’Brien and her son Bobby Cafagna travelled from Perth to witness the recovery, with the family describing the moment as a fitting end to a story that began when a 19-year-old became lost in the darkness.
Article Summary: Brian O’Brien was 19 when he entered the Yarrangobilly Caves in New South Wales in December 1953. A short exploration turned into a three-day fight for survival. The pair became separated inside East Deep Cave, and O'Brien eventually lost the carbide lamp that was his only source of light after slipping and falling. He spent about 74 to 75 hours underground with little food and only a small amount of water before rescuers found him. After surviving his ordeal, he went on to become a prominent space scientist specialising in lunar dust.

Article Title: Kentucky man won $167.3 million Powerball jackpot in 2025; now arrested for fifth time after being found intoxicated in Walmart car park
Article Text:
Police found Kentucky Powerball winner asleep in a running Mustang

How James Farthing won Kentucky's record Powerball prize

Florida arrest came shortly after the jackpot win

February arrest involved an intimidation charge

Burglary and marijuana charges followed in March

July domestic violence case involved strangulation allegations

Fifth arrest adds to Farthing's legal cases

James Farthing, a Kentucky man who won a $167.3 million Powerball jackpot in April 2025, has been arrested for the fifth time since claiming the prize. The latest arrest took place on September 20, 2026, after deputies reportedly found him asleep inside a running Ford Mustang in a Walmart car park in Georgetown. Authorities charged him with being intoxicated in a public place following reports of alcohol-related impairment. The incident adds to a series of legal cases involving Farthing since his jackpot win. He had shared the historic prize with his mother, Linda Grizzle, after purchasing a $2 ticket from a Georgetown retailer.Earlier incidents included an April 2025 arrest in Florida, where Farthing was accused of kicking a sheriff’s deputy during an altercation. He later pleaded guilty to misdemeanor battery and obstruction or resisting arrest. In February 2026, he faced an intimidation charge, followed by burglary and marijuana-possession charges in March after being accused of entering a Lexington home and stealing $12,000. In July, he was arrested on domestic violence-related charges, including first-degree strangulation and fourth-degree assault. Farthing has pleaded not guilty to the domestic violence charges.The latest incident began shortly before 3 a.m. on Sunday, September 20, when a caller reported a white Ford Mustang stopped in the middle of an intersection in Georgetown, Kentucky. The vehicle later moved to a Walmart car park on Osborne Way, according to the arrest citation reported by WKYT.Deputies arrived and found the Mustang parked near an electric vehicle charging station with its engine running. Farthing was reportedly asleep in the passenger seat. Officers knocked on the window several times before he woke up.The arrest citation described several signs of impairment, including the smell of alcohol and marijuana, bloodshot and watery eyes, slurred speech and difficulty maintaining balance. Farthing was subsequently charged with being intoxicated in a public place and taken to the Scott County Detention Center.According to the arrest report, Farthing told deputies that a woman had driven him to the car park and left him there. Authorities reviewed surveillance footage, which reportedly showed no one exiting the Mustang after it entered the car park.Farthing purchased the winning Powerball ticket from Clark's Pump N Shop in Georgetown. The ticket matched the required numbers in the April 26, 2025 drawing, resulting in a $167.3 million jackpot.The Kentucky Lottery identified the prize as the largest Powerball jackpot ever won in the state. Farthing and his mother, Linda Grizzle, claimed the winnings together and announced that they would share the fortune.The win brought significant attention to the family, while Farthing later appeared in news reports concerning several encounters with law enforcement in Kentucky and Florida.Farthing's first reported arrest after winning the lottery took place in Florida in April 2025. Authorities accused him of battery involving a law enforcement officer and resisting arrest following an incident at a hotel.According to the Associated Press, officers said Farthing kicked a deputy in the face during an altercation and attempted to flee. He faced charges connected to the confrontation.The Independent later reported that Farthing pleaded guilty in the case and received a sentence of time served and $1,000 in fines.In February 2026, Farthing was arrested in Georgetown on a charge involving intimidation of a participant in a legal process. The case followed a report from a woman who contacted emergency services and said she feared for her safety.According to People, police investigated an incident at Farthing's home and reportedly found a woman hiding under a desk. Authorities also searched the property and allegedly discovered a handgun, ammunition, marijuana and drug paraphernalia.Farthing faced additional charges in March 2026 in connection with allegations of burglary and marijuana possession. Authorities accused him of entering a Lexington home and stealing approximately $12,000 in cash.The Guardian reported that investigators used security camera footage during the investigation. Farthing was later reportedly located at a casino.Local news reports said the burglary and marijuana charges were dismissed in May. The dismissal applied to those specific charges and did not resolve his other legal cases.In late July 2026, Farthing was charged with first-degree strangulation and fourth-degree assault following a reported domestic violence incident in Scott County.Police said a woman reported that a verbal argument became physical after a boating trip. According to the arrest report, she alleged that Farthing placed both hands around her neck and restricted her breathing. Authorities also reported visible marks on her neck.Farthing pleaded not guilty through his legal representative. A judge set his bond at $15,000 and ordered him to avoid contact with the alleged victim. He was also required to wear an electronic monitoring device with a notification feature.The September arrest is the fifth reported arrest involving Farthing since he won the Kentucky Powerball jackpot in 2025.The latest case concerns public intoxication in Scott County and follows the July domestic violence-related arrest. His legal proceedings remain separate from the lottery win, which he shared with his mother.As of September 23, 2026, the public intoxication case remained pending in Scott County District Court, with no confirmed outcome of the scheduled arraignment.The jackpot that promised a new beginning has instead been followed by a string of legal troubles. Fortune's wheel turns without warning, and wealth offers no guarantee of a steady life.
Article Summary: James Farthing won a $167.3 million Powerball jackpot in April 2025. He has been arrested for the fifth time since claiming the prize. The latest arrest took place on September 20, 2026, after deputies reportedly found him asleep inside a running Ford Mustang in a Walmart car park in Georgetown. Authorities charged him with being intoxicated in a public place following reports of alcohol- related impairment.

Article Title: In 2017, a Utah nonprofit founder reopened an abandoned fire station; then made it a job-and-housing base for up to five homeless families at once.
Article Text:
REPRESENTATIVE IMAGE: An old Utah fire station was transformed into a community centre serving families experiencing homelessness | Pexels

REPRESENTATIVE IMAGE: An old Utah fire station was transformed into a community centre serving families experiencing homelessness | Pexels

The firehouse became a daytime base

Ogden Fire Station No. 2, pictured here, is a historic fire station in Ogden, Utah. The former Fire Station No. 3 was later converted into a community resource centre | Wikimedia Commons

The arrangement was temporary

Nancy Davis Broderick was looking for a building that could serve families experiencing homelessness when she came across Ogden, Utah's abandoned Fire Station No. 3. The former firehouse had showers, a kitchen, restrooms, storage rooms, a washer and dryer, and office space, and in 2017, the city agreed to let her organization, Family Promise of Ogden, use the building without paying rent for a year.Broderick founded Family Promise of Ogden in 2014, according to KSL, as a local affiliate of the national Family Promise network, and it was designed to help families that are experiencing homelessness move toward employment and permanent housing. She had spent more than two years looking for a suitable facility by the time she found the fire station.The building is at 340 South Washington Boulevard and was initially Fire Station No. 3. It was no longer being used by the fire department, but much of the infrastructure needed for a family resource center was already there. The city agreed to provide the building rent-free, while Family Promise would cover utilities and maintenance.Families could use the former fire station to search for jobs and housing, meet caseworkers, attend classes, shower and do laundry during the day, and at night, participating churches provided places for the families to sleep, and rotated responsibility among congregations.KSL reported that the day center could serve up to five families at a time, and Broderick hoped the program could help more than 50 families during the first year of the lease.The arrangement also meant the organization could use the fire station without taking on a conventional commercial lease. Ogden City Council records show that the proposed agreement was a no-cost lease running from April 1, 2017, through March 30, 2018, with Family Promise being responsible for utilities and maintenance. Family Promise could use the showers and restrooms, while the kitchen could support the center's daily operations, and rooms that had previously served firefighters were repurposed for computers, children's activities, casework and other services. Family Promise's own history says the organization was formed in 2015 after Nancy and David Broderick, along with local churches and community members, began exploring a program that would allow families experiencing homelessness to remain together while receiving support. In 2016, the organization received nonprofit status, and Ogden City donated a retired fire station for use as its day center and administrative offices.The fire station was never intended to become Family Promise of Ogden's permanent home, and the city approved the one-year arrangement while the organization searched for a longer-term facility. The model depended on cooperation between several parts of the community, with families receiving daytime services at the fire station, and churches supplying overnight accommodations on a rotating basis. Volunteers helped with meals, transportation, children's activities and other parts of the program.The transformation was complete enough for Family Promise to hold a ribbon-cutting ceremony by April 2017, and more than 100 people attended the event, according to KSL. The first families were expected to begin using the center in May. The organization eventually moved to a permanent location, with an Ogden City document from 2019 saying that Family Promise of Ogden opened its new home at 127 24th Street in February that year, which ended the fire station's role as its main facility.The old Fire Station No. 3 therefore served as a temporary piece of infrastructure in the organization's early years, where a retired municipal building turned into a place where families could work with caseworkers, search for jobs and housing, and access basic services while churches provided overnight shelter.
Article Summary: Nancy Davis Broderick founded Family Promise of Ogden in 2014 to help families that are experiencing homelessness move toward employment and permanent housing. She spent more than two years looking for a suitable facility before she came across Ogden, Utah's abandoned Fire Station No. 3. The city agreed to let her organization use the building without paying rent for a year. Family Promise could use the showers and restrooms, while the kitchen could support the center's daily operations.

Article Title: In 2023, a Georgia homeowner went on vacation and returned to a pile of rubble after a demolition crew tore down her family house at the wrong address
Article Text:
AI-generated representative image showing the aftermath of a house mistakenly demolished at the wrong address in an Atlanta residential neighborhood. Credits - Google Gemini

One call to a neighbour altered everything

No apology, just an acknowledgement

AI-generated representative image showing a demolition crew working at a residential property while verifying the site address. Credits - Google Gemini

Not an isolated case

One of the most disconcerting ways for homeowners to discover that something has gone wrong at home is when their vacation ends with a call from a concerned neighbour. The news was as terrible as it could get for Susan Hodgson, a homeowner from southwest Atlanta, in 2023. When she returned from a trip, she discovered that the long-standing family property she had kept locked, insured, and maintained for about fifteen years had been completely demolished by a construction crew that had just gone to the incorrect address.When she returned to Atlanta, her family home was gone, leaving only trash and timber behind. For one thing, the city’s own building laws say this kind of destruction should never happen without a permit. The City of Atlanta's building code requires a permit before any structure can be legally demolished, precisely to prevent situations in which a property owner is given no warning that work is about to begin on their land. In this case, no permit had been filed, as the crew was never supposed to be on that property.And cases like these aren’t as rare as they sound. The same year, a different Georgia homeowner experienced a similar situation when a county-owned demolition team demolished a house he had bought and was renovating, citing an address error again; this time, the demolition was carried out by a government contractor rather than a private company.What both cases share is not just the mistaken address but what came next, or rather, what didn't. Neither homeowner appears to have received prompt compensation or a formal admission of fault from the party responsible, despite a permit being legally required before any demolition, private or government-led, can proceed. That gap between what the law demands before a structure can be torn down and what actually happens once it has been torn down by mistake is where homeowners in situations like these tend to find themselves stuck, left to prove damages after the fact rather than being protected from the loss in the first place.For the Atlanta homeowner, the aftermath was almost as frustrating as the demolition itself. Instead of compensation or even a formal apology from the responsible company, she received a notice from the city threatening code violation citations for the very mess the crew had left behind and for the missing permit paperwork for a demolition she had never authorised in the first place.According to Atlanta's own demolition permit protocols , the required paperwork, including site plans, a current rodent treatment letter, and a plumbing permit for the sewer connection, was never filed before any legal demolition could take place. The city then explained that the issue was a civil dispute between the property owner and the corporation, rather than something it would resolve directly, leaving the homeowner to pursue the contractor through the courts on her own.Such wrongful demolitions fall under a unique area of law. Georgia law says wilfully damaging another person's property without permission can be a criminal offence. If the damage surpasses five hundred dollars, the Georgia General Assembly’s own code structure considers it a more serious concern than a mere misunderstanding. Whether a demolition contractor who genuinely made a good-faith error in the address would be criminally prosecuted is quite a different question and usually boils down to prosecutors weighing intent against mere negligence, but at least the statute makes it clear that tearing down a house without the owner’s consent is not something the law takes lightly. She had kept the family property standing all those years just so she could decide its future herself, only to lose that choice completely because of an error that took a demolition crew a matter of hours to make.
Article Summary: Susan Hodgson's home in southwest Atlanta, Georgia, was demolished by a construction crew that had just gone to the wrong address. The City of Atlanta's building code requires a permit before any structure can be legally demolished. In this case, no permit had been filed, as the crew was never supposed to be on that property. Georgia law says wilfully damaging another person's property without permission can be a criminal offence.

Article Title: In 2025, a Texas woman held the ticket for an $83.5 million lottery win but the state delayed the payout amid its fight over ticket-buying couriers
Article Text:
An Ohio lottery vending machine inside Walmart alongside an image of a lottery ticket. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

Agency already in hot water before freezing

A typical lottery office. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

Commission dissolved amid overhaul

Winning a state lottery jackpot is supposed to be the easy part, with payment following soon after officials verify the ticket and confirm the numbers. But an Austin woman holding a winning ticket from a February 2025 draw instead found herself in a months-long confrontation with the same organisation that was supposed to pay her, one that eventually became entangled in a much bigger dispute over how the state's lottery is administered.The winning ticket, worth 83.5 million dollars, was not bought at a regular lottery retailer but with a courier service, a third-party organization that buys actual tickets on a customer’s behalf after receiving an order online or via app. Since 2019, couriers had been working in Texas without a formal licence, in a murky area authorities long argued they had no jurisdiction to oversee. That changed as lawmakers began questioning the size of the ticket and where it came from.The Texas Lottery Commission said within days that it would consider courier operations illegal under current law and refused to deliver the prize money until state police and the attorney general's office investigated. Lawmakers moved just as quickly, introducing a bill to push a formal ban through the state legislature. The bill analysis conducted for Senate Bill 3070 notes that couriers facilitated two different high profile jackpot controversies within the span of two years.The Texas Lottery Commission had already undergone a formal assessment through the state’s sunset process, a way to regularly evaluate whether an organization still deserved to exist in its current form. The agency had already drawn criticism in a Sunset Advisory Commission staff review issued earlier in 2025, which flagged its uneven and reactive approach to lottery couriers long before the ticket became a flashpoint. Legislators built on that existing criticism, and the bill that followed went well beyond simply outlawing couriers. The measure would disband the Texas Lottery Commission and transfer its duties to the Texas Department of Licencing and Regulation, a state agency that has never conducted a lottery of this kind.The frozen jackpot dispute was finally resolved in the courts more than five months after the original win, and the winner received a lump sum payoff after taxes. But by then, the bigger battle over couriers had already transformed the whole economy in the state. The commission outlawed courier operations in early 2025, and the restructuring bill approved by the legislature was put into law shortly thereafter, abolishing the agency that had regulated Texas lottery sales since the early 1990s.On September 1, 2025, the regulatory responsibility moved to the Department of Licencing and Regulation . The department’s own published overview, available in its official lottery report, illustrates just how much money passes through the system it inherited, with more than 39 billion dollars generated for the state since ticket sales began and more than 21,000 licensed brick-and-mortar retailers, a separate network from the unlicensed couriers now banned.The courier services did not vanish without a fight. At least one big operator has sued the commission before its dissolution, arguing that years of implicit consent could not change overnight without appropriate warning. The company argues that the policy shift should not have happened without warning. What started with a single delayed payoff to a single winner in Austin ended up tearing down the regulatory framework that has controlled the state’s lottery for more than three decades, a much more significant outcome than anyone following the story back in February 2025 would have likely expected.
Article Summary: Texas Lottery Commission dissolved amid overhaul of lottery system. Winner of 83.5 million dollar jackpot in February 2025 found herself in months-long confrontation with agency that was supposed to pay her. Winning ticket was bought by third-party courier service, which had been working in Texas without a formal licence.

Article Title: In 2012, Atlanta opened a major trail on abandoned freight corridors; by 2025, the BeltLine reported 2.5 million visits and an economic report linked the area to 91,000 jobs
Article Text:
The Beltline ran through Ardmore Park in 2017 and the undeveloped stretch of the Beltline behind Piedmont Park in 2006. Credits - Wikipedia

A thesis that would not go to the archives

Tens of thousands of jobs, Millions of visits

Sculpture beneath the Freedom Parkway bridge near Inman Park. Credits - Wikipedia

Opinion divided on further growth

Atlanta has never been an easy city to walk through. Decades of highway construction and suburban growth had isolated many of its inner communities from each other, connected largely by highways meant for automobiles, not pedestrians. That gap lingered in the back of one graduate student's mind in the late 1990s as he investigated a loop of long abandoned freight rail routes surrounding the city's core, corridors that most Atlantans scarcely noticed even when they passed within walking distance of their houses. What began as an academic study would in a decade become one of the biggest urban reconstruction projects in the United States.Ryan Gravel presented his vision in a master’s thesis in 1999 while pursuing combined degrees in architecture and city planning at Georgia Tech. He suggested turning the unused rail loop around Atlanta into a continuous route of trails and light rail, uniting areas divided by infrastructure decisions made in previous decades. Gravel subsequently said he thought the document would sit on a shelf. Instead, a municipal councilwoman noticed, and by the mid-2000s the idea had blossomed into a genuine city-supported program with its own funding structure. Construction on the trail's first stages began in 2011 and 2012, transforming stretches of rusty track into paved walkways for cyclists, joggers and commuters within a few years.It is hard to overstate the scope of what has come since, more than a decade later. The Atlanta BeltLine marked the 20th anniversary of its founding as a formal city program in 2025, using the occasion to highlight how far the corridor has come, according to a press release from Atlanta BeltLine. In that same year, an economic-impact analysis by Philadelphia-based consultancy Econsult Solutions found that activity within the half-mile planning area surrounding the route sustained more than 91,000 jobs and generated roughly 23 billion dollars in yearly economic output for the city. Private investment along the route has reached roughly 14.2 billion dollars, surpassing the original 10 billion dollar private-investment target years ahead of the loop's 2030 completion date.Visitor numbers back up the scale of the transformation. In 2025, the corridor drew more than 2.5 million visits, and well over half came from Atlanta residents rather than tourists, a sign the path has become part of daily life for many citizens rather than just a novelty destination. Independent research groups analysing particular portions have identified similarly high usage patterns. A case study by the Landscape Architecture Foundation of the Eastside Trail found an average of roughly 3,000 users on an ordinary weekday and more than 10,000 on weekend days, as well as quantifiable benefits in tree cover and stormwater management along the route.None of this development has come without consequences. Housing prices near finished pieces of the trail have skyrocketed, and long-time residents in numerous communities have expressed concerns over being pushed out of areas they helped to construct. City authorities have countered with affordable housing set aside funded through the project’s tax allocation district, but advocates say those measures still don’t address the displacement danger the path has helped generate. Even proponents of the project acknowledge that the strain is unlikely to ease as the final sections of the loop are completed towards a target date of 2030.What is tougher to argue with is the magnitude of change that one graduate thesis may effect. A circuit of freight lines that formerly carried little more than the occasional supply train now carries millions of pedestrians and cyclists each year, the light rail Gravel's original thesis envisioned still hasn't been built, though the BeltLine launched a small autonomous shuttle pilot, ATL Spoke, in June 2026 as its first operating transit connection. That’s one of the more dramatic changes in how Atlantans really move through their communities for a city long known for vehicle-dependent sprawl.
Article Summary: Ryan Gravel presented his vision in a master’s thesis in 1999 while pursuing combined degrees in architecture and city planning at Georgia Tech. He suggested turning the unused rail loop around Atlanta into a continuous route of trails and light rail, uniting areas divided by infrastructure decisions made in previous decades. In 2025, the corridor drew more than 2.5 million visits, and well over half came from Atlanta residents rather than tourists.

Article Title: In 2004, Chicago covered a grim rail yard and parking lots with Millennium Park; now more than 20 million people visit its free public spaces each year
Article Text:
Millennium Park in Chicago, showing the Lurie Garden and the curving BP Pedestrian Bridge. Credits - Wikipedia

A park atop a garage

Cloud Gate

and a new type of public gathering spot

Beethoven’s Ninth Symphony is performed for concertgoers at the Jay Pritzker Pavilion in Millennium Park. Credits - Wikipedia

A model for other cities to look at

The area along the northern boundary of Chicago's Grant Park was unwelcoming for much of the 20th century. The location was largely overlooked by a city more concerned with its skyline than its ground-level areas, with commuter rail tracks cutting across it and rows of outdoor parking occupying what little space was left. As early as the 1970s, civic organizations proposed reclaiming the area for public use, but political will and financial resources never quite matched up. That goal didn't really take off until the last years of the 1990s, which paved the way for one of the most talked-about civic revolutions in recent American history.Mayor Richard M. Daley launched the project in 1998, and building began that year on a site that had long been controlled by the Illinois Central Railroad. The planners decided not to just clear the lines and parking lots but to construct a full new park over them with underground parking, an operational commuter rail line and a bus highway underneath. Today, the City of Chicago still refers to the location as one of the largest green roofs of its sort in the country, a fact that still surprises many first-time visitors who assume they are simply standing on solid ground. The park eventually opened in July 2004, four years behind its original schedule and well over budget, though few people walking through it today would guess at the years of wrangling that preceded its completion.But the true attraction was what it had on top of it when the structural work was done. Burnished-steel sculpture soon became the park's unofficial symbol: Anish Kapoor's Cloud Gate, which locals call the Bean, its curved surface mirroring the cityscape for anybody who strolls below.Nearby, Jaume Plensa's Crown Fountain utilizes television screens and flowing water to give kids a place to play that also serves as public art, while Frank Gehry’s Jay Pritzker Pavilion introduced a dramatic, ribboned steel bandshell to what was once a stretch of railway sidings. Landscape architects have pointed to the park as a turning point in how public space is designed and funded. The American Society of Landscape Architects, in reviewing the project years later, noted that the park established a new template for how private and public money could combine to create civic space and how that space could then double as an economic engine for the surrounding district. It was no simple feat to bring art, architecture and engineering together in this way, and it required regular collaboration between the city, private funders and a huge range of designers. That collaborative process is why planners continue to study the park well after Chicago.More than two decades after it opened in 2004, the park's pull hasn't faded: Wikipedia's park profile, drawing on city tourism data, puts annual attendance at roughly 25 million, a figure that makes it one of the most visited metropolitan parks in the United States. A large part of its appeal is access. Almost everything in the park, from summer concerts to art exhibits, is still free, a conscious move that officials believe has helped keep the space genuinely open to the whole city rather than just those who can afford a ticket. The park’s layout of smaller chambers filled with art draws directly on ideas first proposed for Grant Park more than a century ago, giving the contemporary design an unexpectedly deep historical thread, the Chicago Architecture Centre notes.What makes Millennium Park worth returning to today is less the sculpture or the fountain as individual pieces and more what the entire project demonstrated possible. A swath of ground that city planners had dismissed as unbuildable for over a century became, over the course of only a few years, a site that changed the way a generation of architects and city officials think about public land.Since then, other cities have turned to Chicago's example to gauge whether such makeovers are worth the expense and effort. Toronto's city planners, for instance, pointed directly to Millennium Park while pitching their own Rail Deck Park, a proposal to deck over a stretch of downtown rail yards. That legacy appears to extend far beyond the park's own 24.5 acres, for a project that began as a stretch of rail yards and surface parking lots and ended with the cars tucked beneath the park itself.
Article Summary: Millennium Park opened in July 2004, four years behind its original schedule and well over budget. The park's layout of smaller chambers filled with art draws directly on ideas first proposed for Grant Park more than a century ago. Landscape architects have pointed to the park as a turning point in how public space is designed and funded.

Article Title: After rejecting the bus and subway, a New Jersey marketing executive kayaked to Manhattan and walked to work; four years on, his Hudson commute took only 45 minutes
Article Text:
Representative image of a kayaker commuting across the Hudson River toward Manhattan. Image Credits: ChatGPT.

From a late-night bus stop to the Hudson

A 45-minute commute with a very different view

For most commuters, crossing the Hudson River means taking a train, waiting for a bus or paying for a ferry. For Zach Schwitzky, the journey from Hoboken, New Jersey, to Manhattan became a daily paddle. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

When exercise became part of the journey

For most commuters, crossing the Hudson River means taking a train, waiting for a bus or paying for a ferry. For Zach Schwitzky, the journey from Hoboken, New Jersey, to Manhattan became a daily paddle. What began as an unusual response to a frustrating commute became a routine that combined his trip to work with exercise, quiet time and a direct route across the river.According to Gant News, Schwitzky and his friend Erik Barber began kayaking to Manhattan in 2012 after growing tired of their usual commute. Four years later, Schwitzky was still making the crossing, with his journey from home in Hoboken to his workplace taking about 45 minutes in total. He spent roughly 20 minutes kayaking across the Hudson, then walked the rest of the way to his office.The idea came from frustration rather than from a formal transport experiment. Schwitzky and Barber worked in digital media and dealt with the usual hassles of getting between Hoboken and Manhattan. In 2012, they decided to look for a way of crossing the river on their own terms.CBS News notes that their first attempts were far from the polished routine Schwitzky would later describe. The pair had relatively little kayaking experience and initially paddled the Hudson together. They began making the journey in February 2012, sometimes wearing wetsuits as they dealt with the cold water. By June, they were averaging four days a week on the river.The water crossing was less than a mile, but the commute involved much more than paddling. Usually, they set off from Hoboken and headed to Pier 66 near West 26th Street in Manhattan. At times, they would dock their kayaks at the marina, while at other times, they would carry them by pushing them on the street to reach their workplace. At one point, Schwitzky even moved his 12-foot kayak through Manhattan using a dolly. The unusual sight drew plenty of attention along the way. They also had to make logistical arrangements, especially to keep workplace equipment dry.By 2016, the novelty had worn off for Schwitzky. Commuting by kayak had become part of his daily routine. He would spend twenty minutes paddling, after which he would walk to his office and complete his journey in about 45 minutes. The arrangement had clear benefits. Schwitzky was not bound to the schedules of the buses or trains, and could leave work whenever he wished. The commute also doubled as his exercise routine, especially since he worked long hours as an entrepreneur.The river also offered something public transport could not: a quiet sense of escape. Those who set out early could find themselves paddling through morning fog or watching the sun rise as the Manhattan skyline slowly appeared across the water. But the trip came with its own risks. Paddlers had to keep an eye out for water taxis, barges and the wakes they left behind, which could suddenly make the water rough. For that reason, they had to leave before 7 a.m. , before the river became busier with boat traffic.According to research published in Preventive Medicine , walking and cycling to work were linked to better physical wellbeing among working adults, although the study did not find a significant link with mental wellbeing. The research did not look at kayaking, but it helps explain why turning a commute into a form of exercise could have appealed to Schwitzky.For Schwitzky, the kayak was not just a way to get to work. It gave him a chance to exercise, spend some quiet time on the water and clear his head before the working day began. After four years, what had once seemed like an unusual commute had become part of his everyday routine. While other commuters dealt with traffic and crowded trains, Schwitzky simply picked up his paddle and crossed the river.
Article Summary: Zach Schwitzky and his friend Erik Barber began kayaking to Manhattan in 2012 after growing tired of their usual commute. After four years, what had once seemed like an unusual commute had become his everyday routine.
